title: Why long-term rates can rise while the Fed stands still
layers: The 10-year Treasury yield is set by investors buying and selling bonds every day, not by the Fed. It can rise even while the Fed holds its own rate steady.

A long-term yield is roughly the average short-term rate investors expect over the next ten years, plus a term premium: extra pay for locking money up through unknown inflation, government deficits and a flood of new bonds. When inflation expectations rise or the government borrows heavily, buyers demand more, bond prices fall and yields climb.
Lending for ten years is a bet on a decade of inflation and policy. When that future looks less certain, lenders want to be paid for the risk.
The Fed steers the short end of the curve; markets set the long end. Mortgages, corporate loans and stock valuations follow the long end.
